messages.subject: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
parts:
I am doing nested (or hierarchical?) cross-validation.

Let's say that I have two model classes M1 and M2, and in each class there are several models with different number of discrete components k (e.g., components in a mixture model).
I want to infer what's the best model class for a given dataset.

I could just have two super-models and do full MCMC directly in the larger space (treating the number of components as discrete parameters), but that's not viable for various reasons.
So, I am computing the posterior, via MCMC, separately for each model class M and number of components k.

The question is, is it okay to use PSIS-LOO twice here?
As far as I understand, I should do something like two nested leave-one-out CV:
  1. For each model class M,
    • For i = 1..N, where N is the number of data points:
      • remove the i-th data point from the full dataset.
      • Perform PSIS-LOO (or any other method) on the reduced dataset to choose the best number of components.
      • Take the best model and now compute the prediction on the left-out i-th data point via PSIS. This yields the i-th LOO-CV score for the model class.
    • The LOO-CV score of each model class is the sum (or mean) of 1..N LOO-CV scores from the N reduced datasets.
  2. Compare the summed scores of the model classes.
Does this make sense, and is there a reference for an usage of this kind? Any non-obvious caveat?
(I was checking this but it does not seem to cover this case.)

Thanks,
Luigi

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
parts:
Hi Luigi,

Yes, it is sensible to use nested cross-validation here (although
integration over k would be better).

You can't use nested PSIS, because in the inner loop you are
doing model selection (optimisation of k). Importance sampling in PSIS
can be used only when you have samples from the posterior.

I recommend using K-fold-CV (e.g. K=10) in the outer cross-validation.

Not also that, the inner optimisation of k will cause overfitting and
the outer cross-validation is only estimating the amount of
overfitting, but can't prevent the overfitting. In some cases the
overfitting can be really bad. See Piironen & Vehtari, Comparison of
Bayesian predictive methods for model selection, which has been just
published in Statistics and Computing
http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y

Aki

messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: Re: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
parts:
Hi Aki,

thank you for your reply.

You can't use nested PSIS, because in the inner loop you are
doing model selection (optimisation of k). Importance sampling in PSIS
can be used only when you have samples from the posterior.

So, I can definitely use PSIS-LOO for model selection (choice of k) in the inner loop, since I have the posterior for each k.
I understand that I also need a full posterior for PSIS-LOO in the outer loop, but I guess I could still use an approximate posterior?

Possible approximations are:
  1. I just keep the model I select (i.e., the posterior over k has collapsed onto a single model). This is probably bad...
  2. As a possibly better alternative, I can build a rough estimate of the posterior over k based on the exponentiated PSIS-LOO CV score of each k (similar to what Burnham & Anderson suggest for AIC-weighted prediction). Then I can easily produce samples from this "pseudo-posterior". I understand that this is not correct -- it's not even a proper approximation of the marginal likelihood (the log is on the wrong side of the summation, and I am using the posterior over parameters as opposed to the prior). However, it looks like that this pseudo-posterior would have some desirable properties in common with the marginal likelihood (i.e., it punishes bad models, and applies some sort of Occam's razor to complex models).
Supposing that (2) is not insane, could I then proceed with PSIS?
I recommend using K-fold-CV (e.g. K=10) in the outer cross-validation.
Yes, that's the alternative (and long) way to go that I had in mind.

Not also that, the inner optimisation of k will cause overfitting and
the outer cross-validation is only estimating the amount of
overfitting, but can't prevent the overfitting. In some cases the
overfitting can be really bad. See Piironen & Vehtari, Comparison of
Bayesian predictive methods for model selection, which has been just
published in Statistics and Computing
http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y

Oh, this is very serendipitous, thanks!
I will start reading right now.

Thanks,
Luigi
